resources.title: SoK: Membership Inference Attacks on LLMs are Rushing Nowhere (and How to Fix It)
resources.abstract: Whether Large Language models (LLMs) memorize their training data and what this means, from measuring privacy leakage to detecting copyright violations, has become a rapidly growing area of research. In the last few months, more than 10 new methods have been proposed to perform Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) against LLMs. Contrary to traditional MIAs which rely on fixed-but randomized-records or models, these methods are mostly trained and tested on datasets collected post-hoc. Sets of members and non-members, used to evaluate the MIA, are constructed using informed guesses after the release of a model. This lack of randomization raises concerns of a distribution shift between members and non-members. In this work, we first extensively review the literature on MIAs against LLMs and show that, while most work focuses on sequence-level MIAs evaluated in post-hoc setups, a range of target models, motivations and units of interest are considered. We then quantify distribution shifts present in 6 datasets used in the literature, ranging from books to papers using a model-less bag of word classifier and compare the model-less results to the MIA. Our analysis shows that all of these datasets constructed post-hoc suffer from strong distribution shifts. These shifts invalidate the claims of LLMs memorizing strongly in real-world scenarios and, potentially, also the methodological contributions of the recent papers based on these datasets. Yet, all hope might not be lost. In the second part of this work, we introduce important considerations to properly evaluate MIAs against LLMs and discuss, in turn, potential ways forwards: randomized test splits, injections of randomized (unique) sequences, randomized finetuning, and several post-hoc control methods. While each option comes with its advantages and limitations, we believe they collectively provide solid grounds to guide the development of MIA methods and study LLM memorization. We conclude with an overview of recommended approaches to benchmark sequence-level and document-level MIAs against LLMs.

resources.title: Membership Inference Attacks Against Machine Learning Models
resources.abstract: We quantitatively investigate how machine learning models leak information about the individual data records on which they were trained. We focus on the basic membership inference attack: given a data record and black-box access to a model, determine if the record was in the model's training dataset. To perform membership inference against a target model, we make adversarial use of machine learning and train our own inference model to recognize differences in the target model's predictions on the inputs that it trained on versus the inputs that it did not train on. We empirically evaluate our inference techniques on classification models trained by commercial "machine learning as a service" providers such as Google and Amazon. Using realistic datasets and classification tasks, including a hospital discharge dataset whose membership is sensitive from the privacy perspective, we show that these models can be vulnerable to membership inference attacks. We then investigate the factors that influence this leakage and evaluate mitigation strategies.

resources.title: Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles
resources.abstract: A membership inference attack allows an adversary to query a trained machine learning model to predict whether or not a particular example was contained in the model’s training dataset. These attacks are currently evaluated using average-case “accuracy” metrics that fail to characterize whether the attack can confidently identify any members of the training set. We argue that attacks should instead be evaluated by computing their true-positive rate at low (e.g., ≤ 0.1%) false-positive rates, and find most prior attacks perform poorly when evaluated in this way. To address this we develop a Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) that carefully combines multiple ideas from the literature. Our attack is 10× more powerful at low false-positive rates, and also strictly dominates prior attacks on existing metrics.

resources.title: Assess privacy risks with the TensorFlow Privacy Report
Privacy Risks from Genomic Data-Sharing Beacons
resources.abstract: The human genetics community needs robust protocols that enable secure sharing of genomic data from participants in genetic research. Beacons are web servers that answer allele-presence queries--such as "Do you have a genome that has a specific nucleotide (e.g., A) at a specific genomic position (e.g., position 11,272 on chromosome 1)?"--with either "yes" or "no." Here, we show that individuals in a beacon are susceptible to re-identification even if the only data shared include presence or absence information about alleles in a beacon. Specifically, we propose a likelihood-ratio test of whether a given individual is present in a given genetic beacon. Our test is not dependent on allele frequencies and is the most powerful test for a specified false-positive rate. Through simulations, we showed that in a beacon with 1,000 individuals, re-identification is possible with just 5,000 queries. Relatives can also be identified in the beacon. Re-identification is possible even in the presence of sequencing errors and variant-calling differences. In a beacon constructed with 65 European individuals from the 1000 Genomes Project, we demonstrated that it is possible to detect membership in the beacon with just 250 SNPs. With just 1,000 SNP queries, we were able to detect the presence of an individual genome from the Personal Genome Project in an existing beacon. Our results show that beacons can disclose membership and implied phenotypic information about participants and do not protect privacy a priori. We discuss risk mitigation through policies and standards such as not allowing anonymous pings of genetic beacons and requiring minimum beacon sizes.

techniques.name: Trigger-Set Model Watermarking
techniques.description: Trigger-set model watermarking lets the owner of a trained classifier show later that a suspect model was copied from theirs, by planting a secret behaviour that only the owner can demonstrate. Before release, the owner chooses a small secret trigger set (in the originating scheme, 100 abstract images), gives each input an arbitrary label unrelated to its content, and trains or fine-tunes the model to return those labels while keeping its accuracy on the real task. In the originating scheme the owner also records cryptographic commitments to the trigger inputs and their labels, which fix the watermark at release so that a trigger set cannot be invented once a dispute has begun. To verify, the owner, or an arbiter shown the opened commitments, sends the trigger inputs to the suspect model through its ordinary prediction interface and counts how many return the assigned labels; an independently trained model matches them at about chance level, so a match rate above a preset threshold is evidence of copying. The technique produces the watermarked model, the commitments and, for each verification, the suspect model's trigger-set accuracy against the threshold.

example_use_cases.description: A medical-imaging company that licenses a chest X-ray classifier for installation on hospital servers, where the weights leave its control, embeds a trigger set before each release and lodges the commitments with a timestamping service. When a near-identical model appears in a rival's product, it queries that product with the trigger images to decide whether there is enough evidence to pursue a licence breach.

Before relying on the watermark in its licence terms, the security team of a retailer that licenses a visual product-search model to partner stores to run on their own servers runs the fine-tuning and pruning attacks in its threat model against the watermarked model, and reports the trigger-set accuracy that survives each, to set the verification threshold and state what the watermark can and cannot evidence.

In a licensing dispute over a satellite-imagery land-use classifier used by a local authority, the developer opens its pre-release commitments to an independent expert, who queries the disputed model's prediction service with the trigger images and reports the match rate against a threshold agreed in advance, without either party handing over model weights.

limitations.description: Removal attacks defeat it in practice. A systematic evaluation of published schemes, trigger-set schemes among them, found none robust against adaptive removal attacks or known ways of deriving a surrogate model, and in the originating paper re-training all layers sharply reduced trigger-set accuracy in models watermarked by fine-tuning. A failed verification does not show a model was not copied, and a robustness claim holds only for the attacks tested.

It evidences copying of the model, not theft through its prediction interface, and needs query access to the suspect. A copy trained on the deployed model's answers (model extraction or distillation) need never see the trigger inputs, and a systematic evaluation found these schemes fail against such surrogates, so extraction needs other defences. A copy used only inside its owner's organisation, or not exposed to queries, cannot be tested at all.

Verification reveals the secret. Sending trigger inputs to a suspect's interface, or showing them to an arbiter, exposes them; an adversary who learns them can fine-tune them away or filter those queries, so verification is in effect single-use unless several trigger sets were embedded or a zero-knowledge protocol is used, both of which the originating paper describes and both of which add work.

Without commitments lodged before release the evidence is weak: whoever holds a copy can embed a second trigger set of their own and claim ownership. In the originating paper's experiments the second set was much less durable under fine-tuning than the first, but that helps only an owner who can show its commitments existed before the disputed model did.

The scheme and its evaluations cover image classifiers that the owner can train or fine-tune with access to the training data. Generative and language models need different designs, and the threshold must reflect the number of classes: an unwatermarked model matched 7.0% of trigger labels on 10-class CIFAR-10 but 1.0% on 100-class CIFAR-100, so chance agreement is far higher with few classes.

resources.title: Protecting Intellectual Property of Deep Neural Networks with Watermarking
resources.abstract: Deep learning technologies, which are the key components of state-of-the-art Artificial Intelligence (AI) services, have shown great success in providing human-level capabilities for a variety of tasks, such as visual analysis, speech recognition, and natural language processing and etc. Building a production-level deep learning model is a non-trivial task, which requires a large amount of training data, powerful computing resources, and human expertises. Therefore, illegitimate reproducing, distribution, and the derivation of proprietary deep learning models can lead to copyright infringement and economic harm to model creators. Therefore, it is essential to devise a technique to protect the intellectual property of deep learning models and enable external verification of the model ownership. In this paper, we generalize the "digital watermarking'' concept from multimedia ownership verification to deep neural network (DNNs) models. We investigate three DNN-applicable watermark generation algorithms, propose a watermark implanting approach to infuse watermark into deep learning models, and design a remote verification mechanism to determine the model ownership. By extending the intrinsic generalization and memorization capabilities of deep neural networks, we enable the models to learn specially crafted watermarks at training and activate with pre-specified predictions when observing the watermark patterns at inference. We evaluate our approach with two image recognition benchmark datasets. Our framework accurately (100%) and quickly verifies the ownership of all the remotely deployed deep learning models without affecting the model accuracy for normal input data. In addition, the embedded watermarks in DNN models are robust and resilient to different counter-watermark mechanisms, such as fine-tuning, parameter pruning, and model inversion attacks.

resources.title: SoK: How Robust is Image Classification Deep Neural Network Watermarking?
resources.abstract: Deep Neural Network (DNN) watermarking is a method for provenance verification of DNN models. Watermarking should be robust against watermark removal attacks that derive a surrogate model that evades provenance verification. Many watermarking schemes that claim robustness have been proposed, but their robustness is only validated in isolation against a relatively small set of attacks. There is no systematic, empirical evaluation of these claims against a common, comprehensive set of removal attacks. This uncertainty about a watermarking scheme’s robustness causes difficulty to trust their deployment in practice. In this paper, we evaluate whether recently proposed watermarking schemes that claim robustness are robust against a large set of removal attacks. We survey methods from the literature that (i) are known removal attacks, (ii) derive surrogate models but have not been evaluated as removal attacks, and (iii) novel removal attacks. Weight shifting and smooth retraining are novel removal attacks adapted to the DNN watermarking schemes surveyed in this paper. We propose taxonomies for watermarking schemes and removal attacks. Our empirical evaluation includes an ablation study over sets of parameters for each attack and watermarking scheme on the image classification datasets CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. Surprisingly, our study shows that none of the surveyed watermarking schemes is robust in practice. We find that schemes fail to withstand adaptive attacks and known methods for deriving surrogate models that have not been evaluated as removal attacks. This points to intrinsic flaws in how robustness is currently evaluated. Our evaluation includes a discussion of the runtime of each attack to underpin their practical relevance. While none of the schemes is robust against all attacks, none of the attacks removes all watermarks. We show that attacks can be combined and find combined attacks that remove all watermarks. We show that watermarking schemes need to be evaluated against a more extensive set of removal attacks with a more realistic adversary model. Our source code and a complete dataset of evaluation results are publicly available, which allows to independently verify our conclusions.

techniques.name: Out-of-Domain Detection
techniques.description: Out-of-domain (OOD) detection identifies user inputs that fall outside an AI system's intended domain or capabilities, enabling graceful handling rather than generating unreliable responses. This technique trains classifiers or uses embedding-based methods to recognise when queries require knowledge or capabilities the system doesn't possess. OOD detection enables systems to explicitly decline, redirect, or request clarification rather than hallucinating answers or applying inappropriate reasoning to unfamiliar domains.

example_use_cases.description: Enabling a medical chatbot specialized in diabetes management to recognize and deflect questions about unrelated conditions, avoiding potentially dangerous medical advice outside its training domain.

Ensuring an educational AI tutor for high school mathematics reliably identifies advanced university-level questions and redirects students to appropriate resources rather than attempting explanations beyond its scope.
Transparently communicating system limitations by explicitly informing users when queries exceed the AI's scope rather than silently providing low-quality responses.

Protecting an insurance claims processing system trained on standard claims from making unreliable decisions on unusual or complex cases (e.g., natural disasters, emerging fraud patterns) by detecting and routing them to specialist adjusters.

Ensuring an autonomous vehicle's perception system detects when it encounters road conditions, weather patterns, or infrastructure types outside its training distribution (e.g., unmapped construction zones, unusual signage), triggering increased caution or human intervention.

limitations.description: Defining precise scope boundaries can be challenging, especially for general-purpose systems or domains with fuzzy edges.
May produce false positives that reject legitimate queries at the boundary of the system's capabilities, degrading user experience.
Users may rephrase out-of-scope queries to bypass detection, requiring robust handling of paraphrases and edge cases.
Difficult to maintain accurate scope detection as systems are updated and capabilities expand or shift over time.
Establishing reliable domain boundaries requires substantial labeled data from both in-domain and out-of-domain examples, which can be expensive to collect and annotate systematically.
Real-time OOD detection adds inference latency (typically 10-50ms per query depending on method), which may impact user experience in time-sensitive applications.

resources.title: An Evaluation Dataset for Intent Classification and Out-of-Scope Prediction
resources.abstract: Task-oriented dialog systems need to know when a query falls outside their range of supported intents, but current text classification corpora only define label sets that cover every example. We introduce a new dataset that includes queries that are out-of-scope—i.e., queries that do not fall into any of the system’s supported intents. This poses a new challenge because models cannot assume that every query at inference time belongs to a system-supported intent class. Our dataset also covers 150 intent classes over 10 domains, capturing the breadth that a production task-oriented agent must handle. We evaluate a range of benchmark classifiers on our dataset along with several different out-of-scope identification schemes. We find that while the classifiers perform well on in-scope intent classification, they struggle to identify out-of-scope queries. Our dataset and evaluation fill an important gap in the field, offering a way of more rigorously and realistically benchmarking text classification in task-driven dialog systems.

techniques.name: Synthetic Data Evaluation
techniques.description: Synthetic data evaluation assesses whether synthetic datasets protect individual privacy while maintaining statistical utility and fidelity to real data. This technique evaluates three key dimensions: privacy (through disclosure risk metrics and re-identification attack success rates), utility (by comparing statistical properties and model performance), and fidelity (measuring distributional similarity to real data). It produces evaluation reports quantifying the privacy-utility-fidelity trade-offs.

example_use_cases.description: Validating synthetic patient data generated for medical research to ensure individual patients cannot be re-identified while maintaining statistical relationships needed for valid clinical studies.

Validating that machine learning models for predicting student outcomes trained on synthetic educational data maintain reliable performance comparable to models trained on real student records, while enabling researchers to share datasets without FERPA violations.
Ensuring fraud detection models trained on synthetic credit card transactions maintain reliable performance comparable to models trained on sensitive real transaction data.

Producing audit-ready evaluation reports for a synthetic financial dataset used to train credit-risk models, demonstrating to regulators (e.g., under EU AI Act or SR 11-7 model risk management guidance) that the training data met documented privacy and quality thresholds, and that all trade-off decisions between privacy protection and model utility were recorded and justified.

limitations.description: Trade-off between privacy and utility means strong privacy guarantees often significantly degrade data quality and analytical value.
Difficult to validate that synthetic data protects against all possible privacy attacks, especially sophisticated adversaries with auxiliary information.
Utility metrics may not capture subtle distributional differences that matter for specific downstream tasks or edge case analyses.
Synthetic data may introduce artificial patterns or miss rare but important real-world phenomena, limiting use for certain applications.
Requires significant domain expertise to properly validate fidelity and utility for specific use cases, as generic statistical metrics may not capture domain-specific requirements or failure modes.

Synthetic data may not preserve fairness properties or bias patterns from original data in predictable ways, requiring careful fairness testing when synthetic data is used to train decision-making models.

resources.title: General and Specific Utility Measures for Synthetic Data
resources.abstract: Data holders can produce synthetic versions of data sets when concerns about potential disclosure restrict the availability of the original records. The paper is concerned with methods to judge whether such synthetic data have a distribution that is comparable with that of the original data: what we term general utility. We consider how general utility compares with specific utility: the similarity of results of analyses from the synthetic data and the original data. We adapt a previous general measure of data utility, the propensity score mean-squared error pMSE, to the specific case of synthetic data and derive its distribution for the case when the correct synthesis model is used to create the synthetic data. Our asymptotic results are confirmed by a simulation study. We also consider two specific utility measures, confidence interval overlap and standardized difference in summary statistics, which we compare with the general utility results. We present two contrasting examples of data syntheses: one illustrating synthetic data that is evaluated as being useful by both general and specific measures and the second where neither is the case. For the second case we show how the general utility measures can identify the deficiencies of the synthetic data and suggest how this can inform possible improvements to the synthesis method.

A Multifaceted benchmarking of synthetic electronic health record generation models
resources.abstract: Synthetic health data have the potential to mitigate privacy concerns in supporting biomedical research and healthcare applications. Modern approaches for data generation continue to evolve and demonstrate remarkable potential. Yet there is a lack of a systematic assessment framework to benchmark methods as they emerge and determine which methods are most appropriate for which use cases. In this work, we introduce a systematic benchmarking framework to appraise key characteristics with respect to utility and privacy metrics. We apply the framework to evaluate synthetic data generation methods for electronic health records data from two large academic medical centers with respect to several use cases. The results illustrate that there is a utility-privacy tradeoff for sharing synthetic health data and further indicate that no method is unequivocally the best on all criteria in each use case, which makes it evident why synthetic data generation methods need to be assessed in context.

resources.title: Generating and Evaluating Synthetic UK Primary Care Data: Preserving Data Utility & Patient Privacy
resources.abstract: There is increasing interest in the potential of synthetic data to validate and benchmark machine learning algorithms as well as reveal any biases in real-world data used for algorithm development. This paper discusses the key requirements of synthetic data for such purposes and proposes an approach to generating and evaluating synthetic data that meets these requirements. We propose a framework to generate and evaluate synthetic data with the aim of simultaneously preserving the complexities of ground truth data in the synthetic data whilst also ensuring privacy. We include as a case study, a proof-of-concept synthetic dataset modelled on UK primary care data to demonstrate the application of this framework.

techniques.name: Canary Exposure Testing
techniques.description: Canary exposure testing measures how strongly a training procedure makes a generative sequence model, such as a language model, memorise rare sequences, by planting random secrets (canaries) in the training data and scoring how much the trained model favours them over values it never saw. Because the secrets are random and their values known, the result is calibrated in a way that tests on real records are not and can be compared across model versions, training settings and numbers of repetitions; unlike extraction or membership inference testing of a finished model, it requires control of the training run, and unlike differential privacy auditing, which also plants records, it gives a memorisation score rather than a statistical bound on epsilon. The tester chooses a format such as 'my account number is' followed by a blank, fills the blank with random values to make several canaries, inserts each into the training data a chosen number of times (for example once, ten times and a hundred times), and trains with the settings used in production. Each canary is then ranked by how probable the trained model finds it compared with every other possible filling of the blank, and its exposure is the base-2 logarithm of the number of possible fillings minus the base-2 logarithm of that rank: about 1 for a canary the model treats like any other value, rising to its maximum when the canary is the model's top choice, the level at which a search over the possible fillings can extract it outright. For large spaces of values the rank is estimated by fitting a distribution to the probabilities of a sample of alternatives, and results are usually plotted as exposure against number of insertions.

example_use_cases.description: An email provider training a reply-suggestion model on users' messages inserts seven-word canaries with random middle words between 1 and 10,000 times each into a training run with the production settings, plots exposure against the number of insertions, and uses the curve to limit how often any rare phrase from a single user may appear in the training data before the model is offered to all users.

A bank's machine learning team choosing among learning-rate schedules and model sizes for an autocomplete model trained on transaction descriptions trains each candidate with the same random account-number canaries at the same insertion counts, and picks the configuration with the lowest exposure among those within a set margin of the best validation accuracy.

A health-records software vendor uses the test as a regression check: each time its clinical-text model is retrained on new notes, the same canaries are inserted at fixed frequencies, and the build fails if the exposure of a canary inserted only once rises above a threshold agreed with the vendor's information governance team.

limitations.description: It needs control of the training run. Canaries must be in the data before training, so the test cannot be applied to a model someone else trained or has already released, and it must use the production settings (optimiser, epochs, model size, hyperparameters), because each of these changes how much is memorised; a test model trained differently says little about the deployed one.

It measures memorisation of the planted secrets, not of the real data. Canaries are random and unlike the rest of the data by design, while real personal data that is repeated, structured or similar to other text can be memorised differently, and the choice of format and of random values changes the result. Low exposure for the canaries does not show that no real record can be extracted.

Exposure is not a privacy guarantee. Its scale depends on the number of possible fillings, so values compare only across canaries with the same number of fillings, and it is not an epsilon: in the original study, models trained with differential privacy at budgets too weak to mean anything (epsilon up to 10^9) still showed negligible exposure, so low exposure cannot stand in for a formal bound.

It needs the model's probability for arbitrary sequences, so a system that returns only its single best output needs a different measure. When the space of possible fillings is too large to score in full, exposure is estimated by fitting a distribution to a sample of alternatives; the estimate depends on that fit holding in the far tail and can exceed the true maximum.

techniques.name: Differential Privacy Auditing
techniques.description: Differential privacy auditing tests whether a training procedure that claims a differential privacy guarantee at a stated budget (epsilon, where smaller means stronger privacy) loses more privacy in practice than the claim allows, by measuring a statistical lower bound on its true epsilon. The guarantee itself comes from a mathematical proof, and membership inference testing reports attack success on real records for any model; the audit instead controls which records are present and asks whether the code that was run honours the proof, so it can expose an implementation bug or accounting error but can never confirm the guarantee. The auditor builds two training sets that differ only by one or a few planted records, called canaries and often crafted to be easy to detect, trains the model many times on each, and applies a fixed test to every trained model to guess whether the canary was present. Confidence intervals for the test's true-positive and false-positive rates, such as Clopper-Pearson intervals for a proportion, are converted into a value of epsilon that the procedure must exceed at a stated confidence level, such as 99 per cent; a bound above the claimed epsilon shows that the claim is false for that implementation. Because hundreds of training runs are costly, a later design needs only one: many canaries are each included or left out at random, the test guesses which were included, and the share of correct guesses gives the bound, which is looser than the many-run design's.

example_use_cases.description: Before an NHS trust releases a readmission-risk model trained with an open-source differential privacy library at a claimed epsilon of 3, its data science team audits the exact code and settings: it trains several hundred models with and without a planted mislabelled record and signs off only if the 99 per cent lower bound stays below 3, recording that the audit could have caught a violation but cannot prove the guarantee.

The maintainers of a differentially private training library run a white-box audit on every release: the auditor sees each intermediate model update and inserts a gradient crafted to be easy to detect, so a change to the clipping or noise-sampling code that silently weakens the guarantee pushes the lower bound above the budget the library reports and fails the build.

A mobile keyboard team training a next-word model with federated learning under a claimed user-level guarantee adds simulated canary users to its single production training run, each included or left out at random and enough of them that a bound above the claim is reachable, and checks the one-run lower bound against the claim, because retraining the federated model hundreds of times is not feasible.

limitations.description: A result below the claim proves nothing. The bound is only as strong as the audit behind it: weak canaries, a test that sees only the final model, or too few runs or canaries can give bounds far below the claimed epsilon (one library's documented single-run audit with 1,000 canaries reported 0.42 for a model trained at epsilon 68.5, and 5.5 for one trained without differential privacy). Only a bound above the claim is conclusive, and a pass must not be reported as confirming the guarantee.

The number of training runs caps what can be detected. With 500 runs per training set and 99 per cent confidence, the largest bound the original method can report is about 4.5 even if the test never errs, so it cannot show a claimed epsilon of 8 to be false; larger budgets need many more runs or a different design. In the single-run design the number of canaries sets the cap in the same way.

Bounds come close to the claim only under the strongest access. For DP-SGD on natural data, audits match the claimed epsilon when the auditor sees every intermediate update and inserts crafted gradients, the setting the standard proof assumes. With crafted input records, seeing every update helps only slightly over the final model, and with the final model most of the original audit's bounds were roughly 7 to 12 times below the claim. A result holds only for the access and canaries it assumed.

It is expensive. The original method trained 500 models per training set to choose the test's threshold and another 500 per set to estimate its error rates, which is impractical for large models. The single-run design avoids this but gives looser bounds, which weaken further when only the final model is seen and the model cannot memorise all the canaries or other training data is added.

It checks one implementation, configuration and pair of datasets. A change of clipping norm, batch size, random initialisation or library version needs a new audit, and canaries that are typical rather than worst-case can miss a violation that affects only unusual records, giving false confidence about the risk to outliers.

techniques.name: Training Data Extraction Testing
techniques.description: Training data extraction testing measures how much of its training text a generative language model reproduces word for word when it is sampled, without the tester supplying any training record to look for. It differs from membership inference testing, which starts from a candidate record and asks only whether that record was used in training, and from canary exposure testing, which needs secrets planted before training. The tester prompts the model with empty prompts or a few words taken from public text, generates a large volume of output (from tens of millions to billions of tokens) with the sampling settings the deployed system uses, and checks it against the training corpus: any span of at least a fixed length, such as 50 tokens, found verbatim in an index of the corpus, and not low-entropy filler such as repeated characters or lists of numbers, counts as extracted, and personal data is checked by tagging names and identifiers in the output and looking them up in the corpus. Where the corpus cannot be searched, the outputs are ranked by how much more probable the model finds them than a smaller reference model or a text-compression algorithm does, and the top-ranked candidates are checked by hand, for example by web search. The result is the share of generated text copied from training data (under the hand-checked route, the number confirmed among the candidates checked), the number of distinct passages extracted, and the passages themselves, each with a count of the training documents that contain it: a passage found in one or two documents is a privacy finding in a way that a licence or news story repeated thousands of times is not.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's privacy engineering team fine-tunes an open-weight language model on ten years of customer-service chat transcripts to draft replies for agents. Before deployment it generates 50 million tokens from public-text prompts with the production sampling settings, searches an index of the transcripts for 50-token matches, and looks up every account number, name and phone number tagged in the output. It runs the same test on the base model as a control.

A hospital research group that trained a clinical note-completion model on de-identified discharge summaries runs the test before sharing the weights with partner hospitals. Besides searching for verbatim passages of the summaries, it tags patient names, dates of birth and NHS numbers in the generated text and looks each up in the training set, to find identifiers the de-identification step missed and decide whether the summaries must be re-scrubbed and the model retrained.

An AI developer preparing an open-weight release compares two checkpoints, one trained on a deduplicated copy of the pre-training corpus. It generates text from each at budgets of 100 million and 1 billion tokens, counts distinct 50-token passages found verbatim in the corpus, and compares how the counts grow with the budget, not a single rate, before choosing which checkpoint to release and what to say about memorisation in the model card.

A government department running a citizen-facing chat assistant on a model it fine-tuned on casework correspondence repeats the test after every fine-tuning update. Because chat-tuned models can leak little under ordinary prompts yet emit training text once pushed off their chat behaviour, the test also uses prompts asking the assistant to repeat a single word many times, a pattern that made one production assistant reproduce its training data.

limitations.description: The result is a lower bound set by the effort spent. The number of distinct passages extracted keeps growing as more text is generated, and one study found that a model which leaked more than another at a small budget leaked less in total. A clean result, or a comparison of models at one fixed budget, can therefore mislead; report the generation budget and compare models at several budgets.

Much memorised text comes out only after the right prompt. In one study, sampling from short public prompts recovered about a third of the passages a model was known to reproduce when given their true opening words, and a chat-tuned model leaked far less under ordinary prompts than when pushed into repeating a word. A low rate under ordinary prompts is weak evidence that the data cannot be extracted.

The verdict depends on what the output is checked against and on the match rule. A public proxy for an unavailable corpus undercounts (in one study a 9 TB proxy found under half the matches a manual web search found), and a minimum match length long enough to rule out coincidence misses short secrets such as phone or account numbers unless they are tagged and looked up separately. Paraphrased leaks and facts stitched together from several documents are not counted.

It is costly at a useful scale. One study generated a billion tokens per model, and its whole evaluation, including a 45 TB index built over a 9 TB corpus, took three weeks on a large cloud machine. The test also produces copies of any personal data the model leaks, which must be stored, reviewed and deleted under the same controls as the training data.

It shows what the model emits, not what an attacker could infer. It does not say whether a known person's record was used in training, and it gives no bound for data the test did not happen to elicit, so a clean result cannot stand in for a formal guarantee such as differential privacy.

techniques.name: Attacker-Model Re-identification Risk Measurement
techniques.description: Attacker-model re-identification risk measurement estimates, for a table of real records about people that is about to be released or shared, the probability that an attacker who links it with other information could correctly match a record to the person it describes. This record follows the attacker models of El Emam and Dankar (prosecutor and journalist) and of Dankar and El Emam (marketer), as implemented in the ARX tool: the assessor lists the quasi-identifiers (columns such as age, sex, postcode and admission date that an attacker could know or find), groups the records that share the same values on them, and names the attacker being guarded against. For a prosecutor, who knows the target is in the table, a record's risk is one over the size of its group in the table; for a journalist, who does not know this and links to a register of the wider population, it is one over the size of the matching group in that population, estimated with a statistical model when the population counts are not known; for a marketer, who tries to match as many records as possible, the measure is the expected share of records matched correctly. The assessor reports the highest record risk, the average risk and the share of records above a threshold set for the release, which decides whether the table can go out as it is or needs more generalisation or suppression first. It measures how easily records can be matched to people under the stated assumptions, unlike k-anonymity, which transforms the data, and it does not measure what can be learned about someone from values their whole group shares.

example_use_cases.description: A health insurer releasing claims data for a public prediction competition assumes an attacker who knows a neighbour's age, sex and a few of their claims, and measures each record's risk as one over the size of its group among all the insurer's members. It generalises ages and procedure codes until the measured probability of re-identification is below the 0.05 threshold agreed for the release, then checks the result with simulated matching attacks.

A pharmaceutical company sharing participant-level data from a completed trial with external researchers measures risk against the wider population, not the trial sample, because the participants are a small sample of everyone with the condition. It estimates how many records are unique in that population with ARX's uniqueness models and records the quasi-identifiers, attacker model, estimator and threshold in the data-sharing agreement for the researchers' data access committee to review.

A city transport authority planning to give a commuting dataset of home district, work district, age band and usual travel times to a contractor training a demand-forecasting model runs the assessment, finds a large share of records unique on home and work district together, merges small districts before sharing, and re-runs the assessment to confirm that the share of records above its threshold has fallen below the agreed limit.

limitations.description: The numbers are only as good as the list of quasi-identifiers and the attacker model behind them. A column left off the list, or an attacker who knows more (several of a person's hospital visits rather than one), can make records far easier to match than the assessment reports, and the assessor has to guess what other data an attacker holds. Repeating the assessment for stronger attackers, as some releases do with simulated matching, shows how sensitive the result is to these guesses.

It measures the chance of finding which record is a person's, not what can be learned about them. If all 20 records in a group share the same diagnosis, each has a measured risk of 1 in 20, yet anyone known to belong to the group has their diagnosis disclosed. Checks on the sensitive values, such as l-diversity, are needed alongside it when the release contains sensitive columns.

The journalist measure needs to know how common each record's values are in the wider population, which is rarely known and is estimated from the sample with statistical models; an evaluation of four estimators of population uniqueness on six clinical datasets found none accurate in all conditions. A small sample does not make re-identification unlikely in itself: one study estimated that 15 demographic attributes would let 99.98 per cent of Americans be correctly re-identified in any dataset.

There is no universal threshold, and the measure chosen changes the answer. For the same records the prosecutor measure is always at least as high as the journalist measure, so applying it to a release that is a small sample of a population over-protects and strips detail the data's users need; El Emam and Dankar found this effect strongest at small sampling fractions. The threshold, and which measure it applies to, must be justified for each release.

It measures one table as released, at one time. An attacker can combine several releases of the same data, or successive versions of a table that is updated, and longitudinal data, where each person has many events, need the attacker's knowledge of several events to be modelled explicitly. The basic measures do neither, so each additional or updated release needs its own assessment that takes the earlier ones into account.

techniques.name: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent
techniques.description: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) trains a neural network, or another model fitted by gradient descent, so that the finished model carries a formal differential privacy guarantee about the individual examples it was trained on. Differential privacy is more often applied by adding calibrated noise to the answer of a query or to a published statistic; DP-SGD instead changes the training algorithm itself. At each step it draws a random batch, computes the gradient (the direction in which an example pushes the model's parameters) separately for every example, scales down any gradient longer than a fixed clipping bound, adds Gaussian noise proportional to that bound to the sum, and updates the model with the noisy average, so that no single example can move the model by much and what influence remains is masked. A privacy accountant adds up the privacy cost of every step from the noise level, the sampling rate and the number of steps, and reports the total as epsilon and delta: epsilon limits how much more likely any trained model is with a given example in the training data than without it, and delta is a small probability that this limit fails. The output is a trained model with a stated (epsilon, delta) guarantee, which also covers anything later computed from the model, including its predictions.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank wants to give a credit-default model to a partner lender, which will hold the model weights. Its data science team trains the model with DP-SGD in Opacus, with each customer contributing one training example so that the guarantee protects a customer, targets epsilon 2 at a delta below one over the number of customers, and records the noise multiplier, clipping bound, sampling rate and accountant output in the model's release file.

A consortium of hospitals publishes the weights of a chest X-ray classifier so that other hospitals can fine-tune it locally. It trains with DP-SGD using one image per patient, replaces the network's batch normalisation layers with group normalisation as Opacus requires, and publishes the (epsilon, delta) guarantee and its unit, one patient, with the weights so that receiving hospitals can cite it in their own assessments.

A recruitment platform fine-tunes a language model, pretrained on public text, on job applicants' CVs (one per applicant) to suggest skills tags. It fine-tunes with DP-SGD, adds the cost of the hyperparameter search it ran on the CVs to the privacy budget, and compares tagging accuracy with a non-private fine-tune to decide whether the accuracy cost at its chosen epsilon is acceptable.

limitations.description: Clipping and noise reduce accuracy, and the reduction is not shared evenly: classes and groups that are rare in the training data lose the most, so a private model can widen an existing accuracy gap between groups. In the original experiments the drop at epsilon 8 was about 1 percentage point on handwritten digits but about 7 on a harder ten-class image task. Accuracy should be reported per group, and pretraining on public data or more training data is often needed to keep the cost acceptable.

The stated epsilon holds only if the code matches the accountant's assumptions. The usual accountants assume each batch is drawn by including every example independently at random, but many pipelines shuffle the data and cut it into fixed batches; an audit of models trained that way measured privacy loss up to four times the epsilon they reported. A claim should name the sampling method and accountant, and differential privacy auditing can test the figure empirically.

The guarantee protects one training example, not one person. If a patient has ten admissions or a customer hundreds of messages in the training set, their protection is much weaker than epsilon suggests, because the bound loosens with the number of examples they contribute. Capping each person's contribution, or making each person a single example, gives a guarantee at the level of the person, at some cost in data and accuracy.

No agreed value of epsilon makes a model private, and large values are common: the method's original headline results used epsilon 8, at which a training outcome may be about 3,000 times more likely with a given example than without it, and the Opacus image tutorial targets 50. Hyperparameter searches run on the private data also leak information unless their cost is added to the budget. A claim should state epsilon, delta, the unit of privacy and what the budget covers.

Computing a separate gradient for every example costs memory and time; in the original experiments one training epoch went from about 40 to about 180 seconds. Layers that combine examples within a batch, such as batch normalisation, break the per-example bound and must be replaced, for example with group normalisation, so an existing architecture may need changing and re-tuning before it can be trained privately.

resources.abstract: A well-known algorithm in privacy-preserving ML is differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD). techniques.name: k-Anonymity
techniques.description: k-Anonymity is a property that a table of real records about people can be made to satisfy before it is released or shared, in which every record shares its values on the quasi-identifiers with at least k-1 other records, so anyone linking the table to another source on those columns always matches a group of at least k records, which is k people only when each person has one record. Quasi-identifiers are columns that are not names or ID numbers but could be found elsewhere and combined to single a person out, such as date of birth, sex and postcode, and because the data holder chooses them, the protection covers only those columns. To reach a chosen k, each quasi-identifier is coarsened along a hierarchy set in advance (exact age to five-year band, full postcode to district), and the values or records that would still sit in a group smaller than k are suppressed, with a search choosing the coarsening that loses least information. The output is the transformed table of real records made less specific, not artificial ones, together with the k it achieves and a measure of the detail lost. Unlike differential privacy, it gives no bound on what an observer can learn, because it blocks linking on the listed columns but does not stop someone learning a sensitive value that everyone in a group shares.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital trust preparing an extract of emergency attendances for a university research team treats age, sex, postcode district and attendance date as quasi-identifiers, since local news reports and social media posts about incidents often carry them. Using ARX it generalises age to five-year bands and dates to weeks, suppresses the records still in groups smaller than five, and sends the extract with a note of the k achieved, the columns covered and the share of records suppressed.

A national statistics office preparing a scientific-use file of a household survey for registered researchers recodes region and occupation into broader groups in sdcMicro, then applies local suppression until every combination of age band, sex, region and household size occurs at least three times, and publishes the number of suppressed values with the file so that users can judge the effect on their analyses.

A motor insurer sharing a claims table with an analytics firm that will build a fraud-detection model applies 10-anonymity to policyholder age, vehicle model and postcode district. Before release it agrees with the firm that the coarser bands still carry enough signal for the model, and it keeps the generalisation scheme so that later releases are generalised from the same scheme rather than a new one.

limitations.description: k-Anonymity hides which record is a person's, not what their group has in common. If all k records in a group share the same diagnosis, anyone who can place a person in that group learns the diagnosis, and an attacker with extra background knowledge can rule out other members of the group. Extensions such as l-diversity and t-closeness add conditions on the sensitive column for this reason; k-anonymity alone does not prevent sensitive values being disclosed.

The protection covers only the columns the data holder lists as quasi-identifiers, and rests on the holder judging correctly which columns an attacker could find elsewhere. A column left off the list, such as a rare diagnosis that a local newspaper has reported, can still single a record out, and the property says nothing about it. Choosing the list needs a realistic picture of the public, commercial and leaked data an attacker could hold.

Each release is protected only on its own. Two k-anonymous versions of the same data, generalised differently or produced at different times as records are added, can be joined to narrow groups below k, and two releases that keep the rows in the same order can be lined up row by row. Later releases must be built from the first, or treat all its released columns as quasi-identifiers, and row order must be randomised before each release.

With many quasi-identifiers or detailed values such as exact dates and measurements, most records are unique, and reaching k needs coarsening or suppression heavy enough to remove the detail an analysis or model depends on; the method suits continuous variables poorly. Because the suppressed records are those with rare combinations of values, the released table can under-represent exactly the unusual cases a model most needs to handle.

Requiring k within the released table treats the attacker as knowing their target is in it. When the table is a small sample of a larger population, a record unique in the table may match many people outside it, so the requirement over-protects; El Emam and Dankar found this over-anonymisation, and the loss of information it causes, greatest at small sampling fractions. A re-identification risk assessment against the population can justify a lighter transformation.

techniques.name: PII Detection and Redaction in Training Text
techniques.description: PII detection and redaction finds personally identifiable information (PII), such as names, email addresses, phone numbers and account or ID numbers, in a body of text and removes or replaces it before the text is used to train or fine-tune a model, so that the model has fewer personal details to memorise and later reproduce. Presidio, a widely used open-source tool first released by Microsoft and now run as an independent community project, is the reference implementation: each document passes through a set of recognisers, in which a named-entity recognition model (by default an English spaCy model) tags names, places and dates, patterns with checksum or format checks catch structured identifiers such as card and NHS numbers, and nearby words such as 'account' raise a candidate's confidence score. Every detection above a chosen score is then replaced with a placeholder for its type (for example <PERSON>), masked, hashed, encrypted or deleted, and the cleaned corpus goes to training. Because detection is never complete, the procedure ends by measuring recall, the share of identifiers actually caught, for each type on a hand-labelled sample of the same corpus. The evidence it produces is that measured miss rate and the cleaned corpus; unlike differential privacy or synthetic data, it removes real personal details from real text and gives no bound on what remains.

example_use_cases.description: A bank preparing two years of customer-service chat transcripts to fine-tune an assistant runs Presidio with added pattern recognisers for sort codes and its own account-number format, replaces each detection with a type placeholder, and has staff label 500 transcripts by hand to measure recall per entity type. It fine-tunes only once recall for names and account numbers meets the target in its data protection impact assessment, where it records the miss rate.

An NHS trust preparing discharge letters to fine-tune a summarisation model finds on a labelled sample that the default English model misses many names written in clinical shorthand and does not detect ward and bed codes at all. It adds lists of staff names and patterns for local codes, re-measures recall on a fresh labelled sample, and reports the remaining miss rate to its information governance group, which decides whether further controls are needed.

A company building a code-completion model from its internal repositories detects email addresses, IP addresses, keys and passwords with patterns and a trained detector, discards detections that are too short or are private network addresses to cut false alarms, replaces the rest with tokens such as <EMAIL> and <KEY>, and reports precision and recall per type on an annotated set of files kept apart from tuning.

limitations.description: Detection always misses some identifiers, and a model can memorise and reproduce what is missed, especially details repeated across many documents. A study that fine-tuned GPT-2 on court judgments and emails scrubbed with Presidio's default tagger and a second recogniser concluded that scrubbing reduces but cannot fully prevent leakage of personal information; Presidio's README gives no guarantee of finding it all. The evidence is a measured miss rate, not proof that none remains.

It finds only the categories it has recognisers for. On a 2022 benchmark of European Court of Human Rights judgments, Presidio's default setup caught about 70 per cent of identifying mentions but only about 45 per cent of direct identifiers, because it did not recognise case numbers, which identify the applicant on their own. Details that identify someone only in combination, such as a job title, employer and town, are not entity types at all, so redacted text can still point to a person.

The default recognisers are built for general English text. Clinical shorthand, other languages, source code and in-house identifier formats need extra recognisers or a different model, and recall measured on one corpus does not carry over to another, so the labelled sample used for the measurement must come from the corpus being cleaned and be kept apart from any tuning of the recognisers.

Raising recall by lowering the score threshold or switching on broad entity types also removes text that is not personal, such as names of public bodies, laws and places the task depends on, which lowers the value of the data for training. On the court-judgment benchmark, switching on organisation names raised Presidio's recall slightly but cut its precision from about 0.76 to 0.54.

Redaction removes identifiers from the text but does not hide whether a document was used for training, and it gives no formal bound. In the GPT-2 study, membership inference on the scrubbed model still reached an AUC of 0.82, where 0.5 is chance, and adding differentially private training brought it down to 0.5. Claims about membership, or a formal guarantee, need DP-SGD or another method alongside redaction.

techniques.name: SMACTR Internal Algorithmic Audit
techniques.description: SMACTR is an internal audit procedure for AI systems, proposed by Raji and colleagues in 2020, in which an audit team inside the developing organisation but separate from the product team examines a system during development and before launch against the ethical objectives and requirements the organisation has declared for it. The audit runs in five stages, each producing set documents. In Scoping, auditors review the product requirements and the declared objectives and write an ethical review of the use case, drawing in independent domain experts and marginalised groups, and a social impact assessment; in Mapping, they map the people involved, review existing design records, interview the engineers and begin a failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), a systematic review of the foreseeable ways the system could fail and their effects, used to rank risks for testing. In Artefact Collection, a checklist confirms that the expected development documents, such as model cards and datasheets, exist; in Testing, auditors run tests chosen from the FMEA's priorities, such as adversarial probing with tailored inputs, and rate each risk high, mid or low from its likelihood and severity in an ethical risk analysis chart; in Reflection, they set the results against the declared objectives, finalise the risk analysis and agree a remediation plan with the engineering team. The documents are kept in an algorithmic design history file, from which the auditors write a summary report that leadership can use to decide whether the system launches, changes or is abandoned.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer's internal audit team audits a claims-triage model before launch. Interviews in Mapping reveal that a field used as a proxy for chronic illness was dropped late without the requirements being updated; the FMEA ranks under-prioritising complex claims as the top risk, so Testing concentrates on claims from people with several conditions, and the summary report goes to the risk committee with a remediation plan and a recommendation to delay launch.

A software company's responsible-AI audit team audits a customer-support chatbot. Artefact Collection finds no datasheet for the fine-tuning conversations, so the auditors require the product team to write one before testing; prompts drawn from the FMEA then test whether the bot discloses other customers' account details or gives poorer answers to customers writing in non-standard English, and the ethical risk chart and remediation plan record what must change before release.

A government digital service's audit team, which reports to the agency's chief risk officer rather than to the delivery programme, audits an in-house model that prioritises housing repair requests before it replaces manual triage. The chief risk officer uses the summary report to decide whether the model goes live, and the design history file and report are filed where the agency's external auditors and ombudsman can later inspect them.

limitations.description: The auditors are employees of the organisation they audit and share its interests; the authors acknowledge that independence is hard to keep and that audits risk becoming reputation management. Findings carry more weight when the audit team reports outside the product's management line and the design history file can be examined by an outside party.

The system is judged against the ethical objectives the organisation declares for it, which the authors note have been criticised as vague, and the paper leaves open what level of performance, for example how close to parity across groups, counts as acceptable. A clean audit shows consistency with the standards and thresholds the organisation chose to declare, and says nothing about any external standard it did not adopt.

The Testing stage prescribes no particular tests; the authors expect tests to vary widely by system and to follow the FMEA's priorities. What the audit can show about the system's behaviour therefore depends on the tests the team chooses, and a failure mode the FMEA did not foresee is likely to go untested.

The audit is deliberately slow and document-heavy, and the authors note that fast, iterative development is hard to audit. Its results describe the system at the time of the audit, so a model retrained or reconfigured afterwards is not covered unless the relevant stages are repeated.

The paper does not say which systems should be audited or in how much depth, leaving that to the organisation, and it illustrates the procedure only on two hypothetical client projects. Published evidence of how well it finds problems in real systems is limited.

techniques.name: Rolling-Origin Evaluation
techniques.description: Rolling-origin evaluation, also called time-series cross-validation or backtesting, estimates how accurately a forecasting model will predict the future by repeatedly recreating the position it will be in when used: trained only on data up to a point in time, it forecasts the period that follows. The evaluator chooses a first forecast origin (the last time point the model may see) late enough to leave adequate training data, fits the model on the data up to that origin, forecasts every step of a fixed horizon ahead, for example one to seven days, and records the error at each lead time against the values later observed. The origin then moves forward by one step or a block of steps and the process repeats, with the model either refitted at each origin on all the data so far or on a window of fixed length (recalibration, in Tashman's terms), or kept unchanged and simply given the new observations as inputs (updating), whichever matches how it will be maintained in service. Because every forecast uses only data from before its origin, the method avoids the leakage of future information that randomly shuffled cross-validation can cause on time-ordered data, and because it uses many test periods rather than the single one of a fixed train-test split, its result depends less on which period happened to be held out. The output is the forecast error, under whatever error measure suits the forecast, broken down by lead time and by origin date for each candidate model, which supports claims about expected accuracy on unseen future data over a stated horizon and shows how that accuracy varies across seasons and conditions.

example_use_cases.description: A regional electricity distributor deciding whether to replace its regression model for day-ahead substation demand with a gradient-boosted model evaluates both over the last two years, with an origin each day at the time forecasts are issued, a horizon of the next 48 half-hours and weekly refitting, as planned for operation. It compares error at each lead time and in each season, and switches only after finding the new model better in winter peaks as well as on average.

A national weather service's post-processing team testing a machine-learning correction for station temperature forecasts places origins every day over three years, with lead times of one to ten days, and refits the correction monthly as it would in service. Error by lead time and by month shows whether the correction still helps at the longest lead times and whether its gain in winter holds in all three winters rather than one.

A hospital's operations analysts choosing a model to forecast emergency admissions one to fourteen days ahead for staff rotas compare a seasonal statistical model with a neural network, using weekly origins over two years that include two winter peaks. They report error at the seven-day lead time the rota planners use, and keep the simpler model because the neural network's advantage disappears at that horizon.

limitations.description: Refitting at every origin multiplies training cost by the number of origins: daily origins over two years means more than 700 fits. Machine-learning forecasters are often refitted only now and then and otherwise just fed new data, which Hewamalage et al. describe as common practice; that is cheaper but measures something different, so the refit schedule in the evaluation must match the one planned for deployment or the errors do not describe the deployed system.

The time-ordered split prevents leakage only through the split itself. Scaling, smoothing, decomposition, feature selection or tuning done on the whole series before splitting, or features summarising a period not yet over at the forecast time, still let future information in. Hewamalage et al. show a model beating the best possible forecast of a random walk only because a decomposition was fitted to the whole series; every such step must be redone within each origin.

Errors from neighbouring origins share most of their training data and, for multi-step horizons, overlapping test periods, so they are correlated: an average over hundreds of origins is less precise than the count suggests, and the spread across origins is not a confidence interval. Deciding whether one model beats another needs a test designed for serially correlated forecast errors, such as the Diebold-Mariano test, not a plain comparison of average errors.

The first origins have little training data, so their errors can overstate those of a model trained on the full history, and a short series leaves few test periods and a noisy average. For purely autoregressive models (past values as the only inputs) on stationary series, whose errors show no remaining autocorrelation, Bergmeir et al. show that standard k-fold cross-validation remains valid, and Hewamalage et al. recommend it for short series as it uses the data more efficiently.

It measures how the model would have performed over the history available, not how it will perform after a change that history does not contain, such as a new tariff, a replaced sensor or an abrupt structural break; Hewamalage et al. note that no evaluation design can anticipate a break that lies only in the future. Results should be stated for the periods and conditions they cover and repeated as new data arrive.

techniques.name: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
techniques.description: Sanity checks for saliency maps are two randomisation tests that show whether an explanation method's output depends on what a neural network has learned, or would look much the same for a network that had learned nothing. In the model parameter randomisation test, the evaluator recomputes explanations for a fixed set of inputs after replacing the trained weights with random ones, either cumulatively from the output layer down towards the input (cascading randomisation) or one layer at a time with the others left trained (independent randomisation). In the data randomisation test, the evaluator trains a copy of the same architecture on the training data with the labels shuffled, until it has memorised them, and compares its explanations with those of the model trained on the true labels. Similarity between original and randomised explanations is measured with rank correlation, with and without absolute values, and with image similarity scores such as the structural similarity index; a method whose maps stay similar fails, because its output cannot reflect the learned weights or the relationship between inputs and labels, as Guided Backpropagation and Guided GradCAM failed in the original study when the upper layers were randomised, while plain gradients and GradCAM passed. Passing is a necessary condition, not proof of a good explanation: it shows a method responds to the model, not that its explanations are faithful or useful.

example_use_cases.description: A radiology AI group considering saliency maps as a guide to where a chest-radiograph model sees a pneumothorax runs cascading randomisation on the trained network, measuring structural similarity between original and randomised maps after each block. It sets aside methods whose maps stay similar, as several common methods did in a published study of this task, unless a deletion test shows they still track the model, and uses the rest only alongside a separately validated localisation model.

An insurer's fraud analytics team shows investigators attribution scores for each claim flagged by a neural-network model. Before rollout it runs independent layer randomisation, one layer at a time, and checks that rank correlation without absolute values falls for every layer, so that the scores investigators see depend on the trained weights throughout the network rather than mostly on the claim's raw feature values.

A wind-farm operator's reliability team uses a one-dimensional convolutional network on gearbox vibration signals and gives maintenance engineers heatmaps over each signal. It runs the data randomisation test by training the same architecture on shuffled fault labels until it fits them, and keeps only heatmap methods whose maps differ clearly between the two networks, since a map that survives shuffled labels cannot show what the network learned about faults.

limitations.description: Passing is easy for an explanation that carries no information. Binder et al. show that attribution maps with no correlation between neighbouring pixels score well in model randomisation tests, and that top-down randomisation tends to preserve the scale of forward-pass activations, so even a good explanation can change only so much. They argue the test should not alone decide whether a method is kept: two methods that score poorly on it beat several gradient methods in occlusion-based tests.

The verdict depends on how similarity is measured. In the original study, rank correlation with absolute values and structural similarity stayed high for some methods after randomisation while rank correlation without absolute values fell to near zero, because randomisation flipped signs but kept the input's outline. There is no agreed pass threshold and libraries set their own defaults, so the measure, absolute-value setting and threshold must be reported with the result.

The similarity measures are sensitive to noise, so a method with noisy maps looks changed by randomisation partly because of its own noise, and its score is overstated. Later work proposes repairs: averaging each explanation over noisy copies of the input before comparing (Smooth MPRT), or comparing how much more complex the explanation becomes after full randomisation (Efficient MPRT); its authors report more reliable results with both.

The model parameter test needs the weights and a layered network, so it cannot be run on a model reached only through an interface. The data randomisation test needs the training data and pipeline and a network able to memorise shuffled labels; the original study trained to over 95% training accuracy, which for a large model costs a full training run.

Most evidence for the tests comes from image classifiers. Passing says nothing about whether the highlighted regions match what matters in the domain: in a chest-radiograph study, every saliency method, including those that passed the randomisation test, localised abnormalities worse than a dedicated detection or segmentation network.

resources.title: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
resources.abstract:
Saliency methods have emerged as a popular tool to highlight features in an input
deemed relevant for the prediction of a learned model. Several saliency methods
have been proposed, often guided by visual appeal on image data. In this work, we
propose an actionable methodology to evaluate what kinds of explanations a given
method can and cannot provide. We find that reliance, solely, on visual assessment
can be misleading. Through extensive experiments we show that some existing
saliency methods are independent both of the model and of the data generating
process. Consequently, methods that fail the proposed tests are inadequate for
tasks that are sensitive to either data or model, such as, finding outliers in the data,
explaining the relationship between inputs and outputs that the model learned,
and debugging the model. We interpret our findings through an analogy with
edge detection in images, a technique that requires neither training data nor model.
Theory in the case of a linear model and a single-layer convolutional neural network
supports our experimental findings.

Assessing the Trustworthiness of Saliency Maps for Localizing                     Abnormalities in Medical Imaging
Gradient-Based Saliency Maps Are Not Trustworthy Visual Explanations of Automated AI Musculoskeletal Diagnoses
resources.abstract: Saliency maps are popularly used to “explain” decisions made by modern machine learning models, including deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). While the resulting heatmaps purportedly indicate important image features, their “trustworthiness,” i.e., utility and robustness, has not been evaluated for musculoskeletal imaging. The purpose of this study was to systematically evaluate the trustworthiness of saliency maps used in disease diagnosis on upper extremity X-ray images. The underlying DCNNs were trained using the Stanford MURA dataset. We studied four trustworthiness criteria—(1) localization accuracy of abnormalities, (2) repeatability, (3) reproducibility, and (4) sensitivity to underlying DCNN weights—across six different gradient-based saliency methods (Grad-CAM (GCAM), gradient explanation (GRAD), integrated gradients (IG), Smoothgrad (SG), smooth IG (SIG), and XRAI). Ground-truth was defined by the consensus of three fellowship-trained musculoskeletal radiologists who each placed bounding boxes around abnormalities on a holdout saliency test set. Compared to radiologists, all saliency methods showed inferior localization (AUPRCs: 0.438 (SG)–0.590 (XRAI); average radiologist AUPRC: 0.816), repeatability (IoUs: 0.427 (SG)–0.551 (IG); average radiologist IOU: 0.613), and reproducibility (IoUs: 0.250 (SG)–0.502 (XRAI); average radiologist IOU: 0.613) on abnormalities such as fractures, orthopedic hardware insertions, and arthritis. Five methods (GCAM, GRAD, IG, SG, XRAI) passed the sensitivity test. Ultimately, no saliency method met all four trustworthiness criteria; therefore, we recommend caution and rigorous evaluation of saliency maps prior to their clinical use.

sample_claims.text: Every saliency method used in the chest-radiograph review tool produced maps whose structural similarity to the original fell below the agreed threshold once the top blocks of the network were randomised, on a held-out sample of radiographs.

For the fraud model's attribution scores, rank correlation without absolute values between original and layer-randomised attributions is below the threshold set in the validation plan for every layer tested.

Heatmaps from the methods kept for the gearbox dashboard differ between the network trained on true fault labels and the same architecture trained on shuffled labels, by more than the threshold stated in the test report.
